title: Construct the Minimum Bitwise Array I
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<int> ans: n entries → returned output, not counted
- no other containers, no recursion, no auxiliary structures
- not counted: input vector, returned vector
approach: The key insight is that `x OR (x+1)` always produces an odd number: when you add 1 to x, the carry chain flips a run of trailing 1-bits to 0 and the first 0-bit to 1, so the OR fills everything from bit 0 up to that first 0-bit with 1s. For odd `nums[i]`, the lowest 0-bit sits at some position q; the minimum valid x is `nums[i]` with bit (q−1) cleared, computed via `lowestZero = (nums[i]+1) & -(nums[i]+1)` then `ans = nums[i] ^ (lowestZero >> 1)`. Even `nums[i]` (only the prime 2) has no solution since the OR is always odd.
hints: Looking at the examples, what do all the valid nums[i] values (3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 31) share in their binary representation that the invalid value 2 does not?

Bit manipulation: for odd nums[i], isolate the lowest 0-bit via `z = (nums[i]+1) & -(nums[i]+1)`, then clear the bit just below it: `ans = nums[i] ^ (z >> 1)`. For nums[i]=7 (111₂), z=8, ans = 7 ^ 4 = 3.

**Only even prime** - nums = [2], the sole even prime, has no valid answer.
`Input: [2]` → `Expected: [-1]`
⚠️ Bug: skipping the evenness check and applying the formula → lowestZero = 3 & -3 = 1, ans = 2 ^ 0 = 2, returns `[2]`

**Smallest odd prime** - nums = [3], the smallest odd prime.
`Input: [3]` → `Expected: [1]`
⚠️ Bug: using `nums[i] & -nums[i]` (lowest set bit of nums[i]) instead of `(nums[i]+1) & -(nums[i]+1)` → 3 & -3 = 1, ans = 3 ^ 0 = 3, returns `[3]`

**All equal** - every element is the same prime.
`Input: [7,7,7]` → `Expected: [3,3,3]`
⚠️ Bug: clearing the lowest 0-bit itself (`ans = nums[i] ^ z`) instead of the bit below → 7 ^ 8 = 15, returns `[15,15,15]`

**Non-minimal valid answer** - nums[i]−1 is always valid for odd nums[i] but not always minimal.
`Input: [7]` → `Expected: [3]`
⚠️ Bug: returning `nums[i] - 1` for odd nums[i] → returns `[6]`, which satisfies 6 OR 7 = 7 but is not the minimum

followUps.q: What if nums[i] can be any integer up to 10^9 (not just primes)?
followUps.a: The same bit trick applies unchanged. Even numbers still yield -1; odd numbers use (nums[i]+1) & -(nums[i]+1) to find the lowest 0-bit. The primality constraint only guaranteed 2 was the sole even case. TC O(n), SC O(1).

followUps.q: What if nums[i] can be up to 10^18?
followUps.a: Switch to long long to avoid overflow in nums[i]+1. The bit trick (nums[i]+1) & -(nums[i]+1) works identically with 64-bit integers. TC O(n), SC O(1).

followUps.q: What if nums arrives as a stream and you must output each ans[i] immediately?
followUps.a: Each answer depends only on its own nums[i] with no cross-element dependency, so process elements one at a time with O(1) state and emit immediately. No buffering needed. TC O(n), SC O(1).
